name: dnsperf
desc: Measure DNS performance by simulating network conditions
why: A DNS load tester from the OARC crowd that opens a real door into how resolvers behave under pressure.

brief.what_it_is: dnsperf and resperf are two command-line DNS benchmarking tools from DNS-OARC. dnsperf reads a file of DNS queries and sends them to DNS servers, measuring latency and throughput. resperf ramps up the query rate and watches how the response rate holds up, to simulate a caching DNS service. The tools take a query data file and a target server, and output latency and throughput metrics; the homepage says the output is concise and that latency data can feed detailed graphs. Sample query data is published alongside the releases.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the tools make it simple to gather accurate latency and throughput metrics for DNS, so network operators can benchmark their naming and addressing infrastructure and plan upgrades. The README adds that they are meant to simulate typical Internet conditions.
brief.how_it_works: dnsperf "self-paces" the query load to simulate network conditions, and newer versions are multithreaded, with each dnsperf client needing two cores. resperf systematically increases the query rate and monitors the response rate to find where a caching resolver stops keeping up. Per-query latency reporting is available in newer versions.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew is not mentioned in either page. Building needs a C toolchain plus autoconf, automake, libtool and pkgconfig. Libraries: OpenSSL (for TSIG), Concurrency Kit (atomic operations), nghttp2 (DNS-over-HTTPS over HTTP/2). LDNS is optional, for dynamic update support, and json-c is optional, for JSON statistics output. Prebuilt Debian, Ubuntu and RPM packages (CentOS, Fedora, RHEL, SLE, openSUSE) are listed at dev.dns-oarc.net/packages. The source tarball ships with configure, so no autotools are needed for it. No accounts or runtime configuration are mentioned; you supply your own query file and target server.
brief.standout: The tool is a DNS load generator that paces traffic to imitate real Internet query patterns, not just a flood. resperf is a separate ramp-up mode aimed at caching resolvers. Its lineage runs from Nominum to Akamai to DNS-OARC, and the project has sample query data and IPv6 query support.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage lists release 2.16.0 dated August 5, 2026, with a long history of releases since 2019. The Codeberg repo shows 443 commits, 29 tags, 7 open issues, and a latest commit dated 2026-10-13. The README points to issues on Codeberg and a Mattermost chat for support.
brief.caveats: Build needs several C libraries (OpenSSL, Concurrency Kit, nghttp2, plus LDNS and json-c for optional features), so it is not a single-binary install. Each dnsperf client needs two cores. The README's license note says Apache 2.0. The Codeberg page says it needs JavaScript to render, and the README only shows OpenBSD and FreeBSD install lines, not macOS. The brew install is outside what the sources cover. Some older links point to PDFs for v2.0.0.0, which are not the current manuals.

entry.title: dnsperf
entry.tldr: A DNS load generator from DNS-OARC that replays a file of queries at a server and ramps the rate until a resolver stops keeping up.
entry.deeper_look:
dnsperf and resperf are two benchmarking tools for DNS. dnsperf reads a file of queries, sends them to a server, and reports latency and throughput. resperf does something different: it steadily raises the query rate and watches the response rate, to find the point where a caching resolver stops keeping up.

The tools were written to help network operators measure their naming infrastructure and plan upgrades. Per the homepage, they "make it simple to gather accurate latency and throughput metrics for Domain Name Service (DNS)." dnsperf "self-paces" the query load to simulate network conditions, instead of just flooding the target. Newer versions are multithreaded, and each dnsperf client needs two cores.

The idea underneath is that a DNS server's behaviour changes with load, with the mix of queries, and with whether answers are cached. Feeding a resolver a realistic query file and watching where it bends teaches you how resolvers behave under pressure. Sample query data is published alongside the releases, so you have something to replay.

The lineage is Nominum, then Akamai (2006-2018), then DNS-OARC from 2019 onward. It is maintained, with a recent 2.16.0 release listed.
entry.install:
brew install dnsperf
# You supply your own query file and a target DNS server. Only test servers you run or have permission to load.

entry.whats_unique: It paces traffic to imitate real Internet query patterns rather than only flooding a server. resperf adds a separate ramp-up mode aimed at caching resolvers.
entry.caveats: You need a query file and a DNS server to aim at, and each dnsperf client wants two cores; the README's install lines cover Linux and BSD, not Homebrew.
